stances.claim: Justice Secretary (incoming SolGen) Menardo I. Guevarra is correct that the PNP has no legal authority to ban rallies and demonstrations planned for BBM's June 30 swearing-in at the National Museum -- though he correctly added that the right of peaceful assembly 'is subject to reasonable regulations to maintain peace and order, including the requirement to obtain a prior permit.'

There is 'no question about the primacy of the constitutional right of peaceful assembly' -- the real questions are the 'nature and extent of the laws and regulations that the state could approve and implement': who may assemble, where, when, for how long, whether a permit is always indispensable, which entity issues permits, whether foreigners may exercise it, on what kinds of property.

Bayan Muna v. Executive Secretary Ermita (April 25, 2006), penned by 'the erudite Justice Adolfo S. Azcuna' and supported unanimously by the colleagues (including CJ Panganiban as then-chief justice), provides the governing answers -- though 'no single decision can exhaustively answer all the above questions.'

The Bayan Muna summation establishes the core policy: 'in cases involving liberty, the scales of justice should weigh heavily against the government and in favor of the poor, the oppressed, the marginalized, the dispossessed and the weak. Indeed, laws and actions that restrict fundamental rights come to the courts with a heavy presumption against their validity. These laws and actions are subjected to heightened scrutiny.'

The Calibrated Preemptive Response (CPR) policy -- announced in the Malacañang press release of September 21, 2005 'in lieu of maximum tolerance' to disperse 'unlawful mass actions' -- was struck down: 'the so-called [CPR] policy has no place in our legal firmament and must be struck down as a darkness that shrouds freedom. It merely confuses our people and is used by some police agents to justify abuses.'

BP 880 was upheld as constitutional: it 'does not curtail or unduly restrict freedoms; it merely regulates the use of public places as to the time, place and manner of assemblies. Far from being insidious, maximum tolerance is for the benefit of rallyists, not the government.' The delegation to mayors of permit-issuance authority is valid because it is subject to the 'clear and present danger' standard.

Bayan Muna 'goes even one step further' by imposing a 30-day deadline on local governments to designate specific freedom parks per BP 880 Section 15 -- and if no such parks are identified within that period, 'all public parks and plazas of the municipality or city concerned shall in effect be deemed freedom parks; no prior permit of whatever kind shall be required to hold an assembly therein. The only requirement will be written notices to the police and the mayor's office to allow proper coordination and orderly activities.'

notable_anecdotes: The Bayan Muna summation preserved as a long extended quotation -- including the policy that 'the scales of justice should weigh heavily against the government and in favor of the poor, the oppressed, the marginalized, the dispossessed and the weak,' the CPR strike-down as 'a darkness that shrouds freedom,' and the BP 880 affirmation that 'maximum tolerance is for the benefit of rallyists, not the government.' Modeling extended-precedent-quotation as analytical discipline.

CJ's self-citation by the Court itself: 'In several policy addresses, Chief Justice Artemio V. Panganiban has repeatedly vowed to uphold the liberty of our people and to nurture their prosperity' -- preserved as the institutional acknowledgment of CJ's policy contribution.

The 30-day default rule: if LGUs fail to designate freedom parks within 30 days, 'all public parks and plazas of the municipality or city concerned shall in effect be deemed freedom parks' -- a self-executing institutional safeguard that converts LGU inaction into expanded liberty.

one_paragraph_summary: Justice Secretary (and incoming Solicitor General) Menardo I. Guevarra correctly noted that the Philippine National Police has no legal authority to ban rallies and demonstrations planned for President-elect BBM's June 30 swearing-in at the National Museum -- though he added the constitutional caveat that the peaceful-assembly right is 'subject to reasonable regulations to maintain peace and order, including the requirement to obtain a prior permit.' Panganiban affirms the primacy of the right and enumerates the open doctrinal questions (who, where, when, how long, what kind of permit, foreigners, public vs private property), then turns to Bayan Muna v. Executive Secretary Ermita (April 25, 2006) -- penned by 'the erudite Justice Adolfo S. Azcuna' and concurred in unanimously by colleagues including then-CJ Panganiban himself -- as the governing precedent. The decision condemned the Arroyo-era 'Calibrated Preemptive Response' (CPR) policy announced in a Malacañang press release of September 21, 2005 ('CPR will now be enforced, in lieu of maximum tolerance... Unlawful mass actions will be dispersed') and struck it down as having 'no place in our legal firmament... a darkness that shrouds freedom' that 'merely confuses our people and is used by some police agents to justify abuses.' At the same time it upheld Batas Pambansa Blg. 880 (the Public Assembly Act of 1985) as constitutional -- 'it does not curtail or unduly restrict freedoms; it merely regulates the use of public places as to the time, place and manner of assemblies. Far from being insidious, maximum tolerance is for the benefit of rallyists, not the government.' Mayoral permit-issuance authority was valid because subject to the 'clear and present danger' standard. The Court grounded the policy in CJ Panganiban's own prior addresses (which the decision quoted): 'in cases involving liberty, the scales of justice should weigh heavily against the government and in favor of the poor, the oppressed, the marginalized, the dispossessed and the weak. Indeed, laws and actions that restrict fundamental rights come to the courts with a heavy presumption against their validity. These laws and actions are subjected to heightened scrutiny.' The decision 'goes even one step further' by imposing a 30-day deadline on local governments to designate specific freedom parks per BP 880 Section 15 -- and if no such parks are identified within that period, 'all public parks and plazas of the municipality or city concerned shall in effect be deemed freedom parks; no prior permit of whatever kind shall be required to hold an assembly therein. The only requirement will be written notices to the police and the mayor's office to allow proper coordination and orderly activities.'
